I find this to be the central commitment of American STS and the adjacent projects of AI ethics, ontological turn, etc: Reality is basically a projection of identity/ sociopolitical alignments and thus tech is only sociomorphic. This is the new California Ideology.

And so, the mobilization is against the exteriority of tech and indeed exteriority itself. Culture is drawn as a closed loop totality, for which the only outside is another closed loop culture which determines its own unique world in parallel.

The litany of crimes laid at sci/tech is nothing compared to the crimes done in the name of culture and *meaning*.  The accusations against sci/tech amount to an epistemological ad hominem, not a precise critique of anything other than the Humanism they are supposedly defending.

Social reductionism/ cultural determinism are especially keen to debunk the possibility of this exterior, because the premise that there is so much outside of self-referential socio-political interiority would undermine their claim to the throne of symbolic/ ethical arbitration.

For this, the notion that science allows conceptual access to preconditions of the human (and the fundamentally non-human)  is not some sort of  epistemological ideal but a dangerous smokescreen for power.

This is also why American STS is what it is. The critique of ideological distortion of science inverted itself into the committed insistence that science is and must be subsumed by sociopolitical determinism.

Sociomorphic view of tech ("All Tech is Human") lends itself to cultural determinism. It can claim that changing the culture will result in diff tech outcomes because it believes that tech is foremost an extension of underlying cultural dynamics.

kosmos nekros properly identifies this as a kind of mutual surrogacy. Finally, there is no planetary with an extraplanetarity. There is no escape, because there never was an outside to begin with, only thresholds between life and death.

Experimental astronautics also depends on terrestrial tests for extraterrestrial conditions (biopshere 2 for example) as well as extraterrestrial tests for terrestrial conditions (Science on the ISS, for example), each simulating the other in turn,

It shows also the existential threshold of the understanding of life itself as a system, as the systemization of energy such that the moment when something or someone that was alive becomes not alive could be deduced physically. Finally, entropy doesn’t care.

What can a body do? Many things up to the point of this limit, and no more. Past this line, the practical philosophy of experimental astronautics shows the outline of what the human is and what it cannot be, where it breaks down as a system.

For all these reasons and more the question of Death in space, even space as death, is fraught. It means  not ascendence but something much more immanent: a threshold limit condition that defines not the transcendence of the human but the boundaries between life and death.

It is also worth recalling that when the first humans were gazing at the stars, our entire solar system, itself in motion, was in a different location than it is now, and so their sky would look quite alien to us. What seems eternal is sometimes fleeting.

The numinous ocean of the night sky has been not just a map of the ascension, but itself a technology for navigation and orientation. Today we know that the night sky is also a kind of time machine, showing us light from many millions of years ago.

Until quite recently, the presumed architecture of Space was also a sphere, but one in our planet rested. The celestial firmament was a kind of dome or bubble in which Earth sat suspended, and through the holes in its shell shone light from the beyond, a spectacle we call stars.
But when space was “up” it was also Divine. It was the direction of Heaven. It was literally where God lived. It was where you go after you die (and as this project will show,sometimes it still is).

First of all from the perspective of a flat earth from which our intuitive relation to ground evolved, space seems to be “up.” It is, however, more like “out”. From a sphere, one goes “out” into space.

The history of “space” —that is extraterrestrial space, outside the atmosphere of our planet, extending as far as light can reach— is defined by metaphors both grandiose and deeply parochial. e alien to us. What seems eternal is sometimes fleeting.

The spectacle of secession is an understandable projection no doubt. But it is also symptomatic of a deep dichotomization of ‘down here’ vs. ‘up there’ that should itself be the first casualty of going into “space”.

This exit/ no exit referendum framing of what is at stake for Space seems to be more intensely defended as a frame by those unsurprisingly critical of the billionaire-first strategy than it is by those enthusiastic about private space industries.

However, that very premise that the exploration and even migration into space is a matter of ‘exit” from Earth is the wrong framing one that itself must be refused. Space is not about exit or not exit. Space is a given, not an alibi.
This condition is put in peril both by a parade of billionaire stunts as well as the reactions to them that actually accept their premise (while rejecting their claim on it).
For this, what is called “space” or “outer space” is equally important to both. It is a philosophical as well as an astronomic condition for thought.

The stakes of the term “planetarity” -- and the conditions to which it refers-- could not be higher. For our program the term is mobilized in both its astronomical and philosophical senses, one contextualizing and challenging the other.

In moving beyond the sacralized images of the Blue Marble and the human as Vitruvian, our historical and contemporary imaginaries of space open to a new retelling through a systems view of life and death in the kosmos.
Kosmos and Nekros, therefore, emerge as shared boundary conditions that raise questions of the knowing and unknowing of the limits of human knowledge and experience.
How far the human can be untethered from its original context and propagate the planet outwards entails the reassessment of our epistemological frameworks and their implications for design.
This historical interplay between space as both the realm of idealism and the crucible of technological development offers an interpretative framework for approaching questions of human finitude.

The only humans to have died in outer space are the three Russian cosmonauts of the Soyuz 11 Mission, 1971. To die in outer space is to approach two shared unknowns: the limit of the human in terms of its mortality, and our planetary limits in the extension of outer space.
